passages.t: A great man, and a captive girl
passages.happening:
Naaman commands the army of the king of Aram. He is a great man, highly regarded, ‘for through him the LORD had given victory to Aram’ (verse 1). ‘And he was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper’ (verse 1).

Raiders from Aram have carried off a young girl from Israel, and she serves Naaman's wife. She says to her mistress, “If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria, he would cure him of his leprosy” (verse 3). The king of Aram sends Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel and a vast gift: ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold and ten sets of clothing (verse 5). The letter asks the king to cure his servant (verse 6).

The king of Israel tears his clothes. “Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper?” (verse 7). He is sure the king of Aram is picking a quarrel.
passages.hearers:
The Elisha stories move from the prophet's own circle to Israel's enemy. Aram, the kingdom of Damascus, fought Israel for Gilead and the northern borderlands through most of the ninth century BC, with raiding between the larger campaigns, which explains how a band of Arameans could carry off a girl. The kings are not named. The king of Israel is probably Jehoram, about 852 to 841 BC.

The narrator's first verse is startling. Israel's God had given Aram its victories. The word, teshu'ah, means deliverance or salvation, from the same root as the name Joshua. The LORD directs even the victories of Israel's enemies.

The Hebrew word translated leprosy, tsara'at, covered a range of skin diseases and even mold, and it probably did not usually mean what is now called Hansen's disease. In Israel it made a person unclean and kept him out of the community. In Aram it seems not to have barred Naaman from command.

The story is a study in greatness and smallness. It stacks up Naaman's titles and then adds one word, leper. The one who knows the way to healing is a small captive girl. A talent weighed roughly thirty kilograms, so the gift was a king's ransom. The king of Aram thinks a letter and money can buy a cure, and the king of Israel can only panic. He cannot imagine that God might act.
passages.later: Hannah had prayed, ‘The LORD brings death and gives life’ (1 Samuel 2:6). The king of Israel knew the words and did not expect the God who said them to do anything.
passages.asks: A captive girl, with every reason to be bitter, pointed her master to the prophet. Ask how God might use you in a place you never chose. And ask whether, like the king of Israel, you have stopped expecting God to act.

passages.happening:
Elisha hears that the king has torn his clothes and sends word: “Please let the man come to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel” (verse 8). Naaman comes with his horses and chariots to Elisha's door. Elisha does not come out. He sends a messenger: “Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean” (verse 10).

Naaman goes away angry. He thought the prophet would come out, call on the name of the LORD and wave his hand over the spot (verse 11). “Are not the Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?” (verse 12). He turns away in a rage.

His servants come to him and say, ‘My father, if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it?’ (verse 13). So he goes down and dips himself in the Jordan seven times, as the man of God said, ‘and his flesh was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Naaman's expectations were shaped by how healers worked in his world: the prophet would come out, call on his god and wave his hand. Elisha's refusal even to meet him, and the command to wash in a foreign river, struck him as an insult.

Damascus sat in a fertile oasis watered by rivers from the Anti-Lebanon mountains. The Abanah is usually identified with the Barada, which runs through the city, and the Pharpar with a river to its south. The Jordan is muddy and unimpressive for much of its length, which makes his complaint understandable.

The great man must go down into the Jordan, and his flesh becomes like that of a little child, the same Hebrew word for small used of the captive girl. The word for clean, taher, is the language of ritual purity from Leviticus, not only of cure. His healing is given, not bought, and it comes through simple obedience to a word that seemed beneath him. And again the people who show him the way are servants.
passages.later: Jesus, seeing a man with leprosy, ‘reached out His hand and touched the man’ (Mark 1:41) and made him clean.
passages.asks: Naaman nearly missed his healing because the cure seemed too simple and too humbling. Ask what keeps you from receiving what God freely offers. And ask who in your life, like Naaman's servants, tells you the plain truth when your pride is in the way.

passages.t: No God in all the earth but in Israel
passages.happening:
Naaman goes back to the man of God with all his attendants and declares, “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. So please accept a gift from your servant” (verse 15). Elisha answers, “As surely as the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it” (verse 16), and refuses every pressing.

Naaman asks for as much soil as a pair of mules can carry, ‘For your servant will never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god but the LORD’ (verse 17). Then he asks one thing more. When his master goes into the temple of Rimmon and leans on his arm, and he bows down there, ‘may the LORD forgive your servant in this matter’ (verse 18). “Go in peace,” says Elisha (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The question Elijah asked in chapter 1, whether there is no God in Israel, is answered here from an unexpected direction. A foreign general comes to know the LORD while Israel's own king could not imagine that God might act.

In the ancient world gods were commonly tied to particular lands. Naaman's request for Israelite soil, adamah, shows that belief: he wants to worship the LORD on the LORD's own ground back in Damascus. It is imperfect, since the LORD is not bound to a territory, but it is a real attempt to belong to him.

Rimmon was the Aramean storm god, better known as Hadad; Rimmon, thunderer, was one of his titles. Supporting his king's arm in Rimmon's temple was a court ceremony Naaman could not easily escape.
passages.later: Daniel's friends refused to bow at all: ‘we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up’ (Daniel 3:18). And Jesus, in the synagogue at Nazareth, said, ‘there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet. Yet not one of them was cleansed’ (Luke 4:27), except Naaman the Syrian. His hearers were so enraged that they tried to throw him over a cliff.
passages.hard:
Why did Elisha tell Naaman to go in peace, when he asked pardon for bowing in the temple of Rimmon?

Readers have taken Elisha's answer in different ways. Many interpreters see pastoral wisdom. Naaman has just confessed the LORD alone, vowed to sacrifice to no other god, and asks forgiveness because his conscience is troubled. His bow is a court duty, not worship, and Elisha does not load a new believer in a foreign court with rules he cannot yet carry. On this reading the story shows God's patience with a young faith in a hard place.

Other interpreters stress that go in peace was a customary farewell, not an approval of the act, and that Elisha leaves the matter between Naaman and God. Still others note the tension with the first commandment and with Daniel's friends, who would not bow at all. The text does not settle it. What it makes clear is that Naaman's heart has turned to the LORD, and that he knows compromise needs forgiveness.
passages.asks: Naaman knew where his duties would pull against his faith, and he said so. Ask where your work or your setting asks you to bow in ways that trouble your conscience. And ask whether you bring that tension honestly to God, as Naaman did, or hide it.

passages.happening:
Gehazi, Elisha's servant, thinks his master has let the Aramean off too easily. ‘As surely as the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him’ (verse 20). Naaman sees him running and gets down from his chariot. Gehazi tells him that two young men from the sons of the prophets have just arrived, and asks for a talent of silver and two sets of clothing (verses 21-22). Naaman presses two talents on him, and Gehazi hides them in the house (verses 23-24).

Elisha asks him where he has been. “Your servant did not go anywhere,” he replies (verse 25). Elisha says, “Did not my spirit go with you when the man got down from his chariot to meet you? Is this the time to accept money and clothing, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, menservants and maidservants?” (verse 26). The leprosy of Naaman will cling to him and his descendants, and he leaves Elisha's presence leprous, white as snow (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The final scene turns the pattern over once more. Naaman, the outsider, receives grace freely and becomes clean. Gehazi, the insider, grasps at payment and receives Naaman's disease. The disease is the story's frame: it leaves Naaman in verse 14 and clings to Gehazi in verse 27.

Elisha's refusal of payment protected the truth that Naaman's healing was a gift from the LORD, not a service bought from a prophet. Gehazi's lie put a price on it. Greed can be its own idolatry, even in the prophet's own house.

Gehazi has served faithfully until now. He appears again in chapter 8, telling the king about Elisha's deeds, which suggests that the Elisha stories are not told in strict order.
passages.later: Jesus told the Twelve, as he sent them to heal, ‘cleanse the lepers, drive out demons. Freely you have received; freely give’ (Matthew 10:8). Peter told a man who tried to buy the Spirit, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money!” (Acts 8:20).
passages.hard:
Why did Naaman's disease fall on Gehazi and on his descendants?

The text gives Elisha's sentence and no explanation. Gehazi lied to a new believer and to his master, and he turned a free gift of God into a transaction, at the very moment it mattered most that the gift be free. The sentence fits the crime in a way the story wants the reader to feel.

The words about his descendants are harder. Elsewhere the Old Testament itself insists that ‘A son will not bear the iniquity of his father’ (Ezekiel 18:20). The text does not say more, and these notes do not add to it. It gives no one a right to treat a person's illness, or a family's, as punishment for someone else's sin.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Gehazi resented the grace shown to a foreigner and tried to profit from it. Ask where you resent grace shown to someone else. And ask whether you have ever tried to put a price on what God gave you freely.
